title: Komlós conjecture
formal: Is there a real constant \(C>0\) such that for every pair of integers \(m,n\ge1\) and every matrix \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) satisfying \(\sum_{i=1}^m A_{ij}^2\le1\) for each \(j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), there exists a single sign vector \(x\in\{-1,1\}^n\) for which \[\max_{1\le i\le m}\left|\sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij}x_j\right|\le C?\] The constant must be independent of both dimensions and all matrix entries.
definitions: For a real vector \(v=(v_1,\ldots,v_m)\), its Euclidean norm is \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_i v_i^2)^{1/2}\), and its maximum-coordinate norm is \(\|v\|_\infty=\max_i|v_i|\). The columns \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) of \(A\) may be any vectors in \(\mathbb R^m\) with \(\|v_j\|_2\le1\), including zero vectors and vectors with negative or irrational entries. The signed sum is \(Ax=\sum_j x_jv_j\), where every one of the \(n\) coefficients is exactly \(-1\) or \(1\). Define the combinatorial discrepancy \(\operatorname{disc}(A)=\min_{x\in\{-1,1\}^n}\|Ax\|_\infty\); this minimum is attained because there are finitely many sign vectors. The proposition asks for a universal upper bound on this number over all such matrices. The same chosen \(x\) must satisfy every row inequality simultaneously, though it may depend on the full matrix. The column norm bound is individual, not an average across columns; there is no row norm, row-count, rank or sparsity restriction. All matrices are finite, with arbitrary positive dimensions. The task is existence of some finite constant, not determination of the optimal constant and not an algorithm for finding the signs. There is no bit encoding or computational-time restriction on the entries or the sign choice. A fractional vector in \([-1,1]^n\), a vector with unassigned zero coordinates, or independent choices of signs for different rows does not constitute the required witness.

context_blocks.text: Each column represents one choice that can be assigned a plus or minus sign; each row measures the resulting imbalance in one constraint. Euclidean normalization limits the total squared contribution of a single choice across all constraints. The challenge is to control their maximum imbalance with one common assignment. For any fixed matrix the discrepancy is finite; the universal assertion concerns one bound valid for every number of choices and constraints.

If \(B\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}\) is an incidence matrix with at most \(t\ge1\) ones in each column, then \(A=B/\sqrt t\) has column Euclidean norms at most one. A Komlós bound \(C\) would therefore give \(\operatorname{disc}(B)\le C\sqrt t\), which is the Beck–Fiala conjecture. An incidence matrix encodes membership of each of \(n\) elements in each of \(m\) sets. The general real-matrix formulation contains this normalized special case, but does not impose its sparsity or entry restrictions.

Banaszczyk’s 1998 theorem gives the classical \(O(\sqrt{\log n})\) bound in the number of columns. Bansal, Dadush and Garg’s 2019 Theorem 2 gives an efficient randomized algorithm attaining that order. These are full-signing bounds, but their growth with \(n\) leaves the dimension-independent conjecture open. The present card does not add the algorithmic requirement that those stronger constructive results satisfy.

Bansal and Jiang’s original Theorem 1.2 improves the bound to \(\widetilde O((\log n)^{1/4})\), where the suppressed factors are powers of \(\log\log n\). Their August 2026 exposition states the bound explicitly as \(O((\log n)^{1/4}(\log\log n)^{7/4})\). These asymptotic expressions concern sufficiently large \(n\); constants can absorb the finitely many small dimensions. The exponent is one quarter, not four. The bound refutes Hajela’s proposed growing lower bound of order \(\sqrt{\log n}\), but it neither proves nor disproves Komlós’s constant bound.

Ercan’s preprint of 8 September 2026 states, for every admissible \(m\times n\) matrix, \[\operatorname{disc}(A)\le2395\left(1+\log_+(n/9)\right)^{1/4}+2\sqrt2,\qquad\log_+(u)=\max\{0,\ln u\}\quad(u>0).\] This removes the iterated-logarithm factor in the claimed upper bound but still grows with \(n\). The paper reports Lean formalizations with the Bansal–Jiang covariance theorem as an external research-theorem assumption; neither those files nor the new proof were independently verified here. Its existence theorem has no estimated bit-model running time.

Guo, Fang and Lu’s preprint submitted on 10 September 2026 claims the full constant bound: for every admissible matrix, \(\operatorname{disc}(A)<3\sqrt{2\pi}\). Its Theorem 1.1 covers arbitrary real vectors, all positive dimensions and every column norm at most one. If correct, it proves the exact existence target here, and its Corollary 1.2 gives the corresponding Beck–Fiala bound. The authors explicitly make no polynomial-time construction claim. This review checked agreement of the theorem statement with the card, but did not independently verify the complete new proof; the status is therefore uncertain.

As a concrete optimization connection, the ESA 2026 paper by Gribanov and coauthors derives algorithms for integer linear programs whose parameter dependence is expressed using Komlós discrepancy bounds. Its published abstract states that the conjecture would reduce the relevant dependence on the number of constraints to a single exponential, with the other stated input parameters retained. This is a conditional application of the conjecture, not evidence that it has been proved.

why: Komlós asks whether controlling the Euclidean size of each vector is enough to balance all coordinates by signs with a dimension-independent error. This is a central link between vector geometry and simultaneous rounding of linear constraints. It would imply the Beck–Fiala bound for sparse set systems and strengthen discrepancy-based guarantees in optimization.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the proposition with a specified finite real constant \(C>0\), or a Lean-checked proof of its logical negation: for every real \(C>0\) there exist positive integers \(m,n\) and a real matrix \(A\) with all column Euclidean norms at most one, such that for every \(x\in\{-1,1\}^n\) there is a row \(i\) satisfying \(|\sum_j A_{ij}x_j|>C\). Equivalently, a negative answer proves that these discrepancies are unbounded; the dimensions and matrix may depend on \(C\), without an efficient construction requirement. A fixed finite lower bound on the necessary constant does not refute the conjecture. A bound that grows with a dimension, a partial coloring, or a result limited to sparse, random or nonnegative matrices does not prove the universal target. No optimization of the positive constant is required.

progress.text: Banaszczyk obtains the classical \(O(\sqrt{\log n})\) discrepancy bound, as recalled in the inspected 2019 and 2026 primary papers.
Bansal, Dadush and Garg’s Theorem 2 makes the \(O(\sqrt{\log n})\) bound constructive for arbitrary real matrices with column Euclidean norms at most one.

Bansal and Jiang’s 2025 preprint, followed by STOC 2026, improves the general bound to \(\widetilde O((\log n)^{1/4})\). This does not assert a fourth power of a logarithm or a dimension-independent bound.
The authors’ new exposition gives the explicit \(O((\log n)^{1/4}(\log\log n)^{7/4})\) bound and still describes the constant Komlós conjecture as open.

Ercan’s Theorem 1.1 claims an explicit \(O((1+\log n)^{1/4})\) bound without the iterated-logarithm factor. The paper’s reported Lean formalization assumes the earlier covariance theorem; this review has not checked the new proof or built its files. A bound growing with \(n\) leaves the card’s target open.

Guo, Fang and Lu’s Theorem 1.1 claims a dimension-independent bound \(3\sqrt{2\pi}\), which would settle the full conjecture. The statement matches this card, but its new proof is not independently verified here; recorded as an uncertain claimed resolution.

status_note: A full affirmative resolution is claimed by Guo, Fang and Lu in arXiv:2609.11189v1, submitted 10 September 2026. Theorem 1.1 matches every matrix, dimension and normalization in this card and gives discrepancy strictly less than 3 sqrt(2 pi), with no algorithmic requirement. This review checked the target match and stated scope, not the correctness of the complete new proof; the card therefore remains active with uncertain status. The preprint was still at v1 when checked on 14 September. This supersedes the earlier same-day search assessment that had found only the September 8 growing upper bound.

sentences: Komlós asks whether every collection of real vectors of Euclidean norm at most one can be assigned signs so that every coordinate of their sum is bounded by one universal constant.
The dimensions and entries are arbitrary, and the same complete choice of signs must control all coordinates simultaneously.
The positive answer requires some finite constant, without determining the best one or giving an efficient algorithm.
Such a theorem would imply the Beck–Fiala discrepancy bound and strengthen rounding and optimization guarantees.

A complete Lean proof must establish the universal bound or unbounded discrepancy; the 10 September 2026 preprint claims the full positive bound, but this review has not independently verified its proof.
